key_insight: LLM-assisted writing can improve text quality but, when widely shared, it may also homogenize language and reduce population-level stylistic diversity.
engineering_relevance: For AI writing systems, the work highlights a tradeoff between clarity gains and diversity loss, informing model design choices such as shared, recursive, or personalized assistance.
method: Model authors and LLMs as distributions over linguistic features that coevolve through repeated interaction.
Analyze three assistance regimes: fixed shared model, recursively updated shared model, and personalized models with author- and population-level feedback.
Derive equilibria, convergence behavior, and a utility model for conformity versus distinctive style.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports synthetic simulations and theoretical analysis showing distinct long-run diversity outcomes across fixed shared, recursive, and personalized assistance regimes.
watch_item: The framework is abstract and simulation-based, so real-world effects may depend on how linguistic features, incentives, and feedback are operationalized in practice.
paper_title: Linguistic Monoculture in LLM-Assisted Language Use
